Paper: [Chi et al. (2023), Diffusion Policy: Visuomotor Policy Learning via Action Diffusion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.04137).

## Problem

Similar observations can admit several valid action sequences, such as approaching an object from either side.
A policy must represent these alternatives while producing a temporally coherent sequence and responding to new observations.
Diffusion Policy models a conditional distribution over action sequences by learning to remove noise from demonstrated actions. [§§II-C and IV-A](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2303.04137#page=3).

## Previous Attempts

Direct regression trains a model to predict actions from observations with a distance loss.
Under squared error, the best unrestricted point predictor is a conditional mean, which can fall between distinct valid strategies.
Other prior approaches use mixture distributions, discrete action representations, or implicit energy functions.
The paper compares representative baselines. [§I](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2303.04137#page=1).

Diffusion Policy's MSE training objective therefore needs careful interpretation: the supervised quantity is noise, and the denoiser's inputs contain a corrupted action sequence as well as the observation.

## Proposed Solution

Let $O_t$ denote the observation history available at controller time $t$, and let $A_t^0$ be a clean demonstrated action window.
The superscript describes the diffusion noise level; it is not a controller timestep.
A standard scheduled corruption can be written as

$$
  A_t^k=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_k}A_t^0
  +\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_k}\,\epsilon,
$$

where $\epsilon\sim\mathcal N(0,I)$ has the same shape as the action window and $\bar\alpha_k$ specifies the retained signal at noise level $k$.
The denoising network predicts

$$
  \hat\epsilon=\epsilon_\theta(O_t,A_t^k,k).
$$

Training minimises the squared difference between the known sampled noise and the prediction:

$$
  J=\mathbb E\!\left[\|\epsilon-\hat\epsilon\|_2^2\right].
$$

The expectation averages over demonstrations, noise levels, and Gaussian noise; coordinate averaging gives the usual MSE normalisation.
The target is $\epsilon$, not the clean action chunk.
The paper writes the corruption schematically as an additive perturbation in Eq. (5); the coefficients above make the standard noise schedule explicit. [§II-B, Eq. (3), and §II-C, Eq. (5)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2303.04137#page=2).
The [DDPM note](../theory/ddpm.qmd#why-noise-prediction-is-a-variational-objective) distinguishes this simplified noise objective from the timestep-weighted variational bound.
Training minimises an upper bound on negative log-likelihood in the variational formulation; it does not minimise a lower bound on log-likelihood.

At execution time, start from a Gaussian action-shaped sample and iteratively denoise it, conditioned on $O_t$.
The final result $\hat A_t^0$ is the model's generated action sequence.
Only selected actions from this final sequence go to the robot; intermediate noisy iterates are internal computation. [Fig. 3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2303.04137#page=3).

## Why noise MSE can support different action modes

The MSE-optimal noise predictor is a conditional expectation given $(O_t,A_t^k,k)$.
That conditioning includes the current noisy candidate, rather than only the scene.
Different initial candidates can therefore follow different denoising trajectories under the same observation.
The sampler, together with the learned denoiser, produces the action distribution.
The paper illustrates different approach directions in Push-T. [§IV-A and Fig. 4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2303.04137#page=4).

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Derivation: the noise target determines the clean-action estimate"}

For $\bar\alpha_k>0$, rearrange the corruption equation:

$$
  A_t^0=
  \frac{A_t^k-\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_k}\,\epsilon}
  {\sqrt{\bar\alpha_k}}.
$$

Replacing the unknown noise with the predicted noise gives an estimate of the clean action window.
This conversion scales prediction errors by a noise-dependent factor, so noise MSE and direct clean-action MSE are not numerically identical across noise levels.
The sampler uses these predictions internally.

:::

## Observation, prediction, and execution horizons

The paper distinguishes three horizons. [§II-C and Fig. 3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2303.04137#page=3).

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $T_o$ | Number of recent observation steps supplied to the policy. |
| $T_p$ | Number of action steps in the predicted window. |
| $T_a$ | Number of actions executed before replanning. |

A longer predicted window lets the model represent temporal relationships beyond the immediately executed action.
Executing only $T_a$ actions allows the next planning call to incorporate newer observations before the entire prediction window is consumed.
Longer prediction is not automatically more robust, and shorter execution requires more frequent inference.

Action indices must be aligned with the observation history.
The paper's diagram includes history-aligned entries in its prediction window, so the executable segment begins at the current controller time rather than necessarily at array index zero.

## What enters attention and what is denoised

In the main formulation, observations condition the denoising process while the action sequence is the object being denoised.
Future camera images need not be generated. [§II-C](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2303.04137#page=3).

The CNN uses observation features and the diffusion step to modulate action features.
The transformer embeds the noisy action sequence into decoder tokens and uses observation embeddings through cross-attention.
Consequently, its cross-attention queries come from action-side representations, while keys and values come from observation-side representations. [§III-A and Fig. 3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2303.04137#page=3).

The paper motivates the transformer as a way to reduce the temporal CNN's tendency to smooth high-frequency action changes.
This is an architectural motivation supported by particular experiments, not a guarantee that causal attention always preserves sharp changes.
The CNN can still receive goals through FiLM; removing the earlier inpainting-based goal mechanism does not make goal conditioning impossible. [§III-A](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2303.04137#page=3).

The transformer's causal action-attention mask does not turn diffusion sampling into one-action-at-a-time autoregression.
Each denoising iteration processes the action window, and successive iterations refine it along the diffusion index.
The [attention note](../../study-notes/machine-learning/attention.qmd#projections) distinguishes token position, attention masks, and generation order.

## Visual features and the noise schedule

The visual encoder uses ResNet-18 with spatial softmax pooling in place of global average pooling and GroupNorm in place of BatchNorm.
Spatial softmax retains spatial information through feature-location summaries, while GroupNorm uses statistics within channel groups rather than across the batch.
The observation representation can be computed once per planning call and reused across its denoising iterations. [§III-B](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2303.04137#page=4).

The paper chooses a square-cosine noise schedule after empirical comparison.
The schedule determines corruption levels and sampler coefficients; these coefficients should not all be described as learned neural-network parameters. [§III-C](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2303.04137#page=4).

## DDPM, DDIM, and deterministic sampling

The paper uses DDPM-style denoising training and discusses DDIM to accelerate inference by using fewer sampling steps. [§III-D](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2303.04137#page=4).
The main text and appendix report different inference-step settings, so there is no single universal step count for every reported experiment. [Appendix D and Tables VI–VII](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2303.04137#page=14).

DDIM can use a deterministic update when its additional-noise parameter is zero.
Then fixed initial noise, observation, model, and sampling schedule determine the output, assuming deterministic model computation.
Different initial noise can still give different chunks for the same observation.
With stochastic sampling, fixing the initial sample alone is insufficient because later steps also draw noise. [Original DDIM sampling implementation](https://github.com/ermongroup/ddim/blob/main/functions/denoising.py#L8-L29).

## The score interpretation and training stability

A score is the gradient of a log density with respect to the sample, rather than a probability or a gradient with respect to model parameters.
For the Gaussian corruption used above, define $\sigma_k=\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_k}>0$.
The ideal noise predictor determines the score of the noisy conditional action distribution:

$$
  s^*(A_t^k,O_t,k)
  =-\frac{\mathbb E[\epsilon\mid A_t^k,O_t,k]}{\sigma_k}.
$$

Thus, the learned approximation is $s_\theta=-\epsilon_\theta/\sigma_k$; simply writing $s_\theta=-\epsilon_\theta$ omits the noise-level scaling.
A Langevin-style update moves in the positive score direction toward locally increasing log density.
The minus sign in a noise-prediction update is consistent with this negative relationship between score and predicted noise.
DDPM and DDIM updates also contain their scheduled rescaling terms, so the Langevin analogy is not an exact description of every sampler. [§§II-B and IV-D](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2303.04137#page=5).

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Derivation: the normalising constant disappears from an action gradient"}

For an energy model with observation fixed, write

$$
  p_\theta(A\mid O)=\frac{e^{-E_\theta(O,A)}}{Z_\theta(O)}.
$$

Taking a log and differentiating with respect to $A$ gives

$$
  \nabla_A\log p_\theta(A\mid O)
  =-\nabla_A E_\theta(O,A).
$$

The derivative of $\log Z_\theta(O)$ vanishes because it does not depend on the action being differentiated.
It need not vanish when differentiating with respect to the model parameters $\theta$.
This distinction helps explain why learning a denoising score can avoid explicitly estimating an action-space normalising constant in the training objective.

:::

The paper compares diffusion training with an implicit behaviour-cloning baseline that uses contrastive negative actions.
Its observed training stability supports the tested denoising recipe, rather than a guarantee that every energy model is unstable. [§IV-D and Fig. 7](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2303.04137#page=6).

## Evidence

The paper compares task success across state and visual policies, simulated benchmarks, and real manipulation tasks.
Its tables separate best-checkpoint performance from averages over final checkpoints, making evaluation protocol relevant to numerical comparisons. [§V and Tables I–III](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2303.04137#page=6).
The visual-policy comparison shows improvements on tasks including Transport and ToolHang, with results depending on the model variant.
These rollout results do not make lower training noise MSE a guarantee of successful control.
The authors also observe benefits from position-control actions and action-sequence prediction in their settings.
Their explanations involving compounding velocity errors, temporal consistency, and idle segments are mechanisms and empirical findings, not proofs that position control or longer chunks always improve a policy. [§§IV-B–C](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2303.04137#page=4).

## Limitations

Iterative denoising costs inference time, and observations can become stale while a chunk is generated or executed.
Sampling separate chunks also does not inherently guarantee continuity between them.
